title: Error Correction
author: David Van Story
summary: In a guest post for Zach Groshell, engineer David Van Story describes how the team behind the CrushAP physics app rebuilt its error handling around Direct Instruction's correction procedure. Their first designs simply showed the right answer and moved on, and students clicked past it. Hidden timers, click-to-reveal and an AI tutor were all trial-and-error fixes that failed to prove understanding. On the advice of DI expert Jon Owen, they adapted the seven-step verbal procedure into four steps for an individual, screen-based setting: correct, repeat, quick replay after a delay, and a variant at the end. The key principle is that if students do not have to correct a mistake, they will not. Early data shows about 9 in 10 students succeed on the immediate retry and more than 8 in 10 on the delayed variant.
points: Showing the correct answer is not the same as correcting an error; a correction must make the student redo the task and prove it again later.
The adapted four-step procedure combines immediate correction, a how-do-you-know question, a quick replay after a short delay, and a new variant at the end of the lesson.
Asking 'How do you know?' after a repeat distinguishes a student who applies the rule from one who recalls the previous answer.
Hidden timers, click-to-reveal and AI-tutor questioning were reasonable but weaker than the decades-old DI procedure.
Because the student must answer again, every correction now generates data on whether the mistake was actually learned.
quotes: Most learning apps think they correct students’ mistakes. Very few actually do. The industry standard is to show the student the right answer and move them on to the next question.
Students must prove they have corrected their mistake by giving correct responses before they are allowed to move on.
It wasn’t until after many iterations of our own correction procedures that we realized that if a student doesn’t have to correct their mistake, they won’t. This is not a dig. It’s human nature.
All of these solutions were reasonable iterations, but they were trial-and-error designs that did not have the right balance of efficiency and proof of understanding.
A student can pick A because they remember it was A. So after the repeat, we ask: ‘How do you know?’.
The student has to pick the reason, ‘Wider spacing means faster motion’. That tells us whether they’re applying the rule or just recalling the answer.

Now every missed question is corrected and asked again right away, and about 9 in 10 of our students get it right on that retry. More than 8 in 10 still get the question right when it comes back at the end of the lesson
Showing a student the right answer isn’t the same thing as correcting a mistake.
